title: The Prophet's Mosque
hookLine: in Medina, built over his home and beside his grave

lines: A YARD, A SHADE, A DOOR HOME.
cards: Mud bricks. Palm trunks for pillars. Palm fronds for a roof that leaked when it rained.
A man carrying bricks with the others, sleeves dusty, while they sing as they work.
That man, the reports say, is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, newly arrived in Medina, building a place to pray beside the rooms where he will live. No dome. No marble.
A yard, a shade, a door onto his home. Today: the Prophet's Mosque.

teach.h: A YARD THAT BECAME A MOSQUE.
teach.b: In Arabic it's al-Masjid an-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque. It began as that simple yard in Medina, and it wasn't only for prayer.
It was where he taught, where visitors and envoys were received, where the poor sat in its shade, where questions were brought and disputes settled. His home opened right onto it.

teach.h: HIS ROOM, BENEATH THE GREEN DOME.
teach.b: When he died, he was buried in his own room, the room of his wife Aisha, and over the generations the mosque grew outward until that room now lies inside it, beneath a green dome.

Muslims visit Medina, often around Hajj or Umrah, to pray in the mosque and to greet him at his resting place. A hadith in Bukhari says that between his house and his pulpit lies a garden of the gardens of Paradise.
That small stretch of carpet is called the Rawdah, the garden, and visitors hope to pray there. Here's what the place teaches.
A great mosque now covers the spot, but its heart is a home: a man who lived among his people, ate with them, built with them, and is greeted there still.

And the Qur'an gives believers a way to greet him from anywhere: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation."
That asking is called salawat. No one has to be in Medina to send it.
His mosque is in Medina; the greeting can come from any kitchen.

how: Muslims visiting Medina pray in the Prophet's Mosque, hope to pray in the Rawdah between his house and his pulpit, and greet him with salutations at his resting place; everywhere else, they send salawat on him, especially in prayer and on Fridays.

Qur'an 33:56: "Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation."

games.q: the first mosque in Medina is going up, brick by brick. where is the Prophet?
games.why: the reports say he carried bricks alongside his companions as they built.

practice: Picture that first yard, palm trunks and mud walls and a man sitting with his companions in the shade, then the mosque today, the green dome, people standing quietly to greet him.
If you pray, you can say the familiar words Muslims use, Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, O God, send blessings on Muhammad, softly on each out-breath.
If you don't, simply hold the picture of that first yard, and the people who built it.

wordCard.voice: Rawdah, the small stretch of the Prophet's Mosque called a garden of Paradise, where visitors hope to pray. Today's word, closing a week of pilgrims' planes, radio voices, women scholars, a hurting ummah, two billion and two holy mosques.

orig.note: Arabic: the Prophet's Mosque, in Medina.

carryVoice: Your line: his mosque. It began as a yard its own people built together. Go gently.
